author: Fermi

entries.title: He Binds What Is Hurt
entries.alt: Jesus kneels beside a resting sheep and finishes wrapping a bandage around its lower foreleg.
entries.caption_html: The sheep rests while the Shepherd tends its leg. Ezekiel 34:11–16 brings seeking, gathering, rest and healing into one promise of care.
paragraphs_html: Ezekiel begins by confronting shepherds who feed themselves while leaving the flock scattered. In Ezekiel 34:1–6, the failure is specific: the weak are not strengthened, the sick are not cared for, and the lost are not sought. The Lord answers with His own promise to search, gather, feed and bind what is broken. Notice how each promise answers a neglected need.

The chapter finally identifies the flock as people in Ezekiel 34:30–31. Its shepherd imagery helps us consider the care of the Savior, who calls Himself the Good Shepherd in John 10:11–18. His care includes knowing His sheep and freely giving His life for them. Read the two passages together, looking for both tenderness and the cost of faithful care.
entries.reflection_html: Which action in Ezekiel 34:11–16 speaks most closely to a need you carry, and which could shape your care for someone else?

entries.title: Leave Room at the Water
entries.alt: A smaller sheep waits behind two larger sheep at a narrow approach to water, with three more sheep on the bank.
entries.caption_html: The water is close, but the smaller sheep waits behind the others. Ezekiel 34:17–22 asks how members of the flock treat one another.
paragraphs_html: Ezekiel turns from the failed shepherds to harm within the flock. Some have eaten good pasture and drunk clear water, then spoiled what others must use. In Ezekiel 34:17–19, having enough does not excuse making life harder for those who come afterward. The image of crowded water gives that question a visible setting: who can reach what is needed?

The Lord also confronts those who push the weak aside in Ezekiel 34:20–22. He promises to save His flock and judge between its members. Read this beside the promise of one shepherd in Ezekiel 34:23–24. Belonging to the flock carries a responsibility to one another; the passage calls attention to conduct, not to a person’s appearance or size.
entries.reflection_html: Where could you make access easier for another person instead of assuming that an open invitation is enough?

entries.title: Care That Keeps Someone Warm
entries.alt: A man stitches a coat lining while an older woman holds the fabric steady at a table.
entries.caption_html: One pair of hands steadies the coat while another repairs its lining. James 2:14–18 asks what faith does when someone needs warmth.
paragraphs_html: James imagines a brother or sister lacking clothing and daily food. A wish for warmth and peace leaves the need unanswered if nothing useful is offered. In James 2:14–18, faith becomes visible through what a person does. The repair on the table offers a small way to consider that teaching: a skill, some time and careful attention can become practical help.

King Benjamin grounds generosity in our shared dependence on God. Read Mosiah 4:19–21 before his counsel about relief in Mosiah 4:26–27. He names material and spiritual needs, then joins diligence with wisdom and strength. Thoughtful service asks what is needed and what we can actually give, without making assumptions about the person receiving it.
entries.reflection_html: What ordinary skill could you offer this week, after first asking whether it would help?

entries.title: Help With What Is Needed
entries.alt: A man lifts a key ring from a drain with a magnetic tool while a woman points toward the opening.
entries.caption_html: The key ring rises from the drain as two people attend to the same small task. Mosiah 4:26–27 connects willing help with wisdom and order.
paragraphs_html: In Mosiah 4:16–21, Benjamin challenges the impulse to judge someone’s need before offering help. He reminds the people that all depend on God for life and for what sustains it. That humility can change an ordinary encounter: we can listen to what another person needs instead of turning the moment into a judgment about them.

Benjamin’s counsel is both generous and practical. Mosiah 4:26–27 directs relief according to people’s needs and the giver’s means, with diligence that respects strength. A dropped set of keys is a modest example of attention becoming useful. The larger invitation is to offer help that fits the situation, welcomes the other person’s knowledge and follows through carefully.
entries.reflection_html: When someone asks for help, what would let you understand the task before choosing a solution?

entries.title: Make the Word Easier to Hear
entries.alt: An older woman presses an audio player’s large play button while a woman beside her points toward the controls.
entries.caption_html: She tries the player herself while her companion stays beside her. Romans 10:14–17 invites us to consider how the word of Christ reaches people.
paragraphs_html: Paul follows a chain of questions in Romans 10:14–17: how will people call upon someone they have not believed in, and how will they believe without receiving the message? His subject is the preaching of Christ and the faith that responds to it. Helping another person find a usable way to study can serve that purpose through audio, readable text, signed communication or another format they choose.

In John 10:3–5, the sheep recognize their shepherd’s voice and follow him. Jesus returns to knowing and following in John 10:27. Read these words as a relationship of trust and response to Him. In the picture, patient assistance leaves the learner in charge of the controls; the person’s own participation matters as much as completing the setup.
entries.reflection_html: What would make scripture study easier for someone you know, and how could you ask without deciding for them?

entries.title: The Children’s Praise
entries.alt: Three children praise Jesus in the temple as He turns toward two religious leaders.
entries.caption_html: The children lift their voices while Jesus answers the adults beside Him. Read their exchange in Matthew 21:14–16.
paragraphs_html: Matthew places the children’s praise after Jesus enters Jerusalem, cleanses the temple and heals those who come to Him there. In Matthew 21:12–16, the chief priests and scribes see His works and hear the children calling Him the Son of David. Their displeasure becomes a question directed to Jesus. Follow the sequence carefully: the children’s voices belong within a larger scene of the Savior’s authority and mercy.

Jesus acknowledges what the children are saying and answers with scripture about praise from the mouths of little ones in Matthew 21:16. He does not silence them to satisfy the objection. As you study, compare the attention given to their praise with the welcome elsewhere in Mark 10:13–16. Adults can learn from the way Jesus receives children as participants in spiritual life.
entries.reflection_html: How could a child’s sincere prayer, question or testimony receive your full attention?

entries.title: A Game Everyone Can Join
entries.alt: A girl using a wheelchair rolls a blue ball across a table toward a boy while another child waits and an adult moves an unused chair.
entries.caption_html: The ball passes across the table, and each child has a part in the game. Mark 9:33–37 asks us to reconsider what it means to receive a child.
paragraphs_html: The disciples have been arguing about who is greatest. Jesus answers in Mark 9:33–37 by teaching service, bringing a child among them and speaking of receiving that child in His name. The change in focus is striking. Instead of ranking themselves, the disciples are asked to recognize the importance of the person before them.

In Mark 10:13–16, Jesus responds when adults keep children from approaching Him. These accounts can guide the practical choices of a gathering today. Clear space, a reachable table and an activity shaped with the children can help them take part. Notice that the girl in the picture directs the play herself; welcome includes the opportunity to contribute and choose.
entries.reflection_html: In an activity you help plan, who should be asked what would make participation easier?

entries.title: A Small Thing Worth Caring For
entries.alt: A child holds a spool and watches an older woman sew a torn seam in a stuffed bear.
entries.caption_html: The child watches the seam while the stitches draw it together. James 1:19–22 connects attentive hearing with what we do next.
paragraphs_html: James calls his readers to be quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger in James 1:19–22. He then urges them to do the word they receive. Listening is therefore more than waiting for a turn to speak. It can require setting aside a quick dismissal and giving enough attention to understand why something matters to another person.

Jesus takes a child in His arms and speaks of receiving children in His name in Mark 9:36–37. The small repair in this picture offers a place to consider that welcome in daily life. A child’s concern may seem slight to an adult, yet patient attention can communicate respect. Even when a problem cannot be repaired, a child can still be heard and accompanied.
entries.reflection_html: What concern might a child need you to hear fully before you offer advice?

entries.title: Learning to Share
entries.alt: A boy offers a sealed snack packet to a girl across a lunch table while an adult watches nearby.
entries.caption_html: The packet passes between two children who both have lunches before them. Mosiah 4:13–16 joins teaching children with learning to love and serve.
paragraphs_html: Benjamin’s teaching follows his people’s experience of forgiveness through faith in Jesus Christ. In Mosiah 4:1–3, they receive joy and peace of conscience. His later counsel about daily conduct grows from that encounter with mercy. Read Mosiah 4:13–15 and notice how peaceful relationships, children’s needs and teaching them to serve belong together.

The instruction continues by asking adults to help those who need their help in Mosiah 4:16. Children learn from what they see as well as what they are told. An ordinary offer at lunch can open a conversation about asking, sharing and respecting another person’s choice. The point is the willing attention behind the gesture, not the size of the gift or an assumption about someone’s circumstances.
entries.reflection_html: What act of consideration could you model, and how could you help a child notice the other person’s choice?

entries.title: Room for a Quieter Moment
entries.alt: A child seated on a floor cushion reaches toward ear defenders offered by an adult, with a gathering visible through an open doorway.
entries.caption_html: The child reaches by choice while the gathering continues through the open doorway. Mark 10:13–16 invites adults to attend to the welcome they offer.
paragraphs_html: When the disciples turn people with children away, Jesus is displeased. In Mark 10:13–16, He calls the children near, takes them in His arms and blesses them. The adults’ behavior changes who can approach. Study the actions in the passage, then consider the practical barriers a child might encounter in a gathering you know.

Patient listening in James 1:19 can help adults understand what a child is asking for. A quieter place, a pause or a different way to join may be a useful response when chosen with the child. In this scene the open doorway keeps the gathering connected to the quiet corner. Attention can be offered without demanding the same response or pace from everyone.
entries.reflection_html: How could you ask a child what would help them join comfortably, while leaving room for their answer?

entries.title: Come Apart and Rest
entries.alt: Jesus sits in a boat facing a headband-wearing companion while one man rows and another rests behind Him.
entries.caption_html: The shore falls behind the boat as the companions sit together. Read the invitation to rest and what follows in Mark 6:30–34.
paragraphs_html: The apostles return to Jesus and report what they have done and taught. Mark 6:30–32 describes so much coming and going that they have no time even to eat. Jesus invites them to come apart and rest, and they leave by boat. The invitation recognizes the needs of people who have been serving; attending to those needs belongs within the account of their work.

Continue into Mark 6:33–34. People recognize their departure and reach the destination ahead of them. Jesus sees the crowd with compassion and begins teaching them. Rest and compassion both matter in the passage, even though the hoped-for retreat is interrupted. Read the whole movement before turning the invitation into a promise of uninterrupted quiet.
entries.reflection_html: What needed rest could you receive or help another person receive this week?

entries.title: A Pause in the Work
entries.alt: A woman sits with her eyes closed and both hands in her lap beside a still sewing machine and unfinished curtain.
entries.caption_html: Her hands rest away from the needle while the curtain remains on the table. Philippians 4:4–9 invites prayer and thanksgiving within ordinary life.
paragraphs_html: Paul asks the Philippians to bring their requests to God with prayer and thanksgiving in Philippians 4:4–7. The promise centers on God’s peace keeping their hearts and minds through Christ. Read slowly enough to name both parts of that prayer: what you need and what you can give thanks for. The work in the picture remains unfinished, with room for a pause before continuing.

Paul also directs attention toward what is true, honest, just and good, and toward putting learned things into practice in Philippians 4:8–9. Later he speaks of both abundance and need in Philippians 4:11–14. His peace is not described as a life without difficulty. These verses offer a way to pray and act faithfully while circumstances still require care.
entries.reflection_html: What request and what thanksgiving could you bring to God before the next part of your work?

entries.title: Slow Enough to Hear
entries.alt: A man pauses beside a wooden board and a resting sanding block to listen to a teenager.
entries.caption_html: The sanding block rests while attention turns toward the person nearby. James 1:19–22 joins patient hearing with living the word.
paragraphs_html: James places hearing, speech and anger together in James 1:19–20. A quick answer can arrive before we understand what was said; anger can make that failure harder to notice. Pausing a task long enough to listen offers one concrete way to consider his counsel. Look at the stopped work in the picture, then think about the attention a real conversation may require.

The invitation continues into action in James 1:21–22. Receiving the word humbly should change what we do. James later describes wisdom as gentle, merciful and willing to be approached in James 3:13–18. Listening need not solve everything at once to be worthwhile. It can help us understand the next faithful response with more care.
entries.reflection_html: What helps you set a task aside and give someone your attention before deciding what to say?

entries.title: Let Peace Become a Choice
entries.alt: A person turns a speaker dial while a neighbor gestures toward an ear and they look at one another.
entries.caption_html: A hand turns toward the dial during a neighbor’s request. James 3:13–18 describes wisdom by the gentleness and peace it brings.
paragraphs_html: James asks the wise person to show wisdom through good conduct and meekness in James 3:13–16. He contrasts that with envy and strife. The question reaches ordinary disagreements as well as public ones: are we trying to understand and respond, or only to defend our position?

Wisdom from above is peaceable, gentle and full of mercy in James 3:17–18. Benjamin likewise connects a changed heart with living peaceably in Mosiah 4:13. A small adjustment may sometimes express that willingness. The image invites us to consider a response that takes a neighbor seriously, while leaving room for continued conversation when needs differ.
entries.reflection_html: What small change could you consider in a disagreement, and what still needs to be understood together?

entries.title: He Makes Wars Cease
entries.alt: A broken bow, a broken spear and a charred wheel lie still on open ground.
entries.caption_html: The weapons lie broken beside a charred wheel. Psalm 46:6–11 places stillness beside the Lord’s power to bring war to an end.
paragraphs_html: Psalm 46:1–3 opens with God as refuge while earth and water are in upheaval. In Psalm 46:6–9, the view widens to raging nations, shaken kingdoms and the end of war. The broken bow and spear belong to that movement. Read these verses before the familiar command to be still, so the psalm’s concern for the whole earth remains in view.

The command in Psalm 46:10–11 is joined to knowing God and to His exaltation among the nations. The psalm closes with His presence and refuge. Its stillness reaches beyond a private moment of calm: it turns our attention toward the Lord amid upheaval and conflict. Let that wider setting shape your prayer for people whose lives are touched by violence and displacement.
entries.reflection_html: How does reading Psalm 46:6–11 together change what you hear in the words “be still”?
